---
title: "Plan and Structure Your Course"
subtitle: "Decide what learners should be able to do, then build the chapter list"
---

::: {.objectives}
**In this chapter**

- Write learning objectives that say what a learner can *do*
- Cut a topic into chapters of a sensible size
- Find the four places that make up the project's skeleton
- Add, reorder and remove chapters
- Start your own course from the empty chapter skeleton
:::

## Plan on paper first

The most common mistake in online courses is starting with the material: "I have
forty slides, let me put them online." Start with the learner instead. Three
questions, in this order:

1. **Who is it for, and what do they already know?**
2. **What should they be able to do afterwards?** Not "know about" or
   "understand", but do.
3. **How will they, and you, find out that they can?**

Only then decide what to teach. Planning backwards from the outcome like this is
sometimes called *backward design* [@wiggins2005understanding], and it removes
most of the material you would otherwise have felt obliged to include.

### Writing objectives that can be checked

An objective is useful when you can imagine the question that tests it. Vague
verbs cannot be tested; concrete verbs can [@anderson2001taxonomy].

| Vague | Concrete |
|---|---|
| Understand hand hygiene | List the five moments for hand disinfection |
| Know the consent process | Explain to a patient, in plain words, what they are consenting to |
| Be familiar with the system | Enter a new patient record without help |
: Turning vague objectives into checkable ones {#tbl-objectives}

Aim for three to six objectives per course and two to four per chapter. They go
at the top of the page in the blue **objectives** panel, and they become your
quiz questions later.

### Cut it into chapters

A chapter should be one topic that a learner can finish in a single sitting,
roughly **15 to 30 minutes**. This is a rule of thumb, not a law, but there is
good reason behind it: people can hold only a few new things in mind at once, so
material that introduces one idea at a time, and lets the learner use it before
adding the next, is easier to learn from [@sweller1988cognitive].

Inside a chapter, follow the same rhythm every time. Learners then always know
where they are:

1. Objectives (what this chapter is for)
2. Explanation in short sections, each with its own heading
3. A **key point** box for the one thing to remember
4. Questions to check understanding

That last step is not decoration. Answering a question about something you just
read helps you remember it far better than reading it again
[@roediger2006test]. Put the questions in.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Use the worksheet

Before creating any file, fill in this table on paper. If you cannot complete a
row, that is the part of the course to think about next.

| Chapter title | Objective (what can the learner do?) | How will they check it? | Length |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | |
:::

## The four places that matter

Everything in the project is either a chapter, a setting, a picture or the
appearance. You only need to know four places:

| Where | What it holds | You edit it |
|---|---|---|
| `01-….qmd`, `02-….qmd`, … | The chapters, one file each | Constantly |
| `_quarto.yml` | The settings: course title, chapter order, footer | When you add or reorder chapters, and once at the start |
| `images/` | Pictures, and the logo | When you add pictures |
| `assets/` | Colours, fonts and quiz behaviour, already set up in the university's corporate design | Never, unless you are asked to |
: The project skeleton {#tbl-skeleton}

Besides these: `index.qmd` is the landing page, `glossary.qmd` and
`references.qmd` are the reference pages, `slides/` holds lecture slides, and
`docs/` is where the finished website appears. Do not edit anything in `docs/`.

## Name your files

Chapter files are named with a number, then a short description:
`03-write-text.qmd`. The rules are boring but they prevent trouble:

- Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens only. No spaces, no umlauts.
- The number keeps them in order in the *Files* panel. It does **not** control
  the order on the website; the settings file does.
- A file whose name starts with an underscore, like `_draft-chapter.qmd`, is
  **ignored** when the website is built. Use that for unfinished work.

## The chapter list: `_quarto.yml`

Open `_quarto.yml`. Most of the file you can leave alone. The part that matters
for structure is the `sidebar:` block, which is the chapter list learners see on
the left of every page:

```yaml
  sidebar:
    style: docked
    contents:
      - index.qmd
      - section: "Basics"
        contents:
          - 01-first-steps.qmd
          - 02-the-workflow.qmd
      - section: "Practice"
        contents:
          - 03-exercises.qmd
```

Read it top to bottom and it matches the sidebar exactly: a landing page, then a
group called *Basics* with two chapters, then a group called *Practice* with one.

::: {.callout-warning}
## This file is strict about spaces

Indentation carries meaning here. Use **spaces, never the Tab key**. Each level
is indented two spaces further, a dash is followed by a space, and a colon is
followed by a space. When in doubt, copy an existing line and change only the
words.
:::

### Add a chapter

1. Copy `_chapter-skeleton.qmd`, and name the copy, say, `04-feedback.qmd`.
2. Open it, change the `title:` at the top and write the chapter.
3. In `_quarto.yml`, add one line in the right place in the list:
   `- 04-feedback.qmd`, indented to match its neighbours.
4. Render.

### Reorder, group or remove

- **Reorder**: move the line up or down in the list.
- **Group**: put chapters under a `- section: "Name"` block, as above.
- **Remove**: delete its line from the list, then delete the file (or put an
  underscore in front of its name to keep it as a draft). If you delete the file
  but leave the line, the render will complain that it cannot find it.

## The top menu

The bar across the top has a few links (*Course*, *Slides*, *Glossary*). They are
listed under `navbar:` in the same file, in the same style. Keep it short: three
or four links. The chapters belong in the sidebar, not here.

## Start your own course

You have two sensible ways to begin.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Keep this course as your manual

Make a **copy** of the whole project folder for your own course, and keep the
original untouched. Then you can consult this course while you work on yours.
This is what we recommend for a first course.

## Start from an empty project

1. Copy the project folder and rename it as in Chapter 1.
2. In `_quarto.yml`, replace the chapter list with your own (start with just
   `index.qmd` and one chapter).
3. Delete the eight chapter files of this course, or put an underscore in front of
   them to keep them out of the build.
4. Create your first chapter from `_chapter-skeleton.qmd`.
5. Edit `index.qmd` for your own course, and change the title, description and
   footer in `_quarto.yml`.

:::

## The landing page

`index.qmd` is the first thing a learner sees. It should answer five questions
in a few lines each: *What is this course? Who is it for? What will I be able to
do afterwards? How long does it take? What do I need beforehand?* Put the
objectives panel and a short route through the chapters on it. This course's own
landing page is a working example.

## Check your understanding

::: {.quiz-score}
:::

::: {.question}
Which of these is a learning objective that can be checked?

- [ ] Understand the principles of good communication
- [ ] Be aware of the risks of the procedure
- [x] Explain the three main risks of the procedure to a colleague
- [ ] Appreciate the importance of documentation

::: {.feedback}
Only the third names something a learner *does* that you could ask a question
about. "Understand", "be aware of" and "appreciate" describe an inner state you
cannot observe.
:::
:::

::: {.question}
You rename `05-quality.qmd` to `_05-quality.qmd`. What happens at the next render?

- [ ] It appears at the top of the sidebar
- [x] It is skipped, so it is not built into the website
- [ ] The render fails
- [ ] It is published with a "draft" label

::: {.feedback}
A leading underscore tells the build to ignore a file. It is the simplest way to
keep unfinished work in the project without publishing it. If the chapter is
still listed in `_quarto.yml`, remove that line too.
:::
:::

::: {.question}
The order of chapters in the sidebar is decided by:

- [ ] The numbers in the file names
- [ ] The alphabetical order of the titles
- [x] The order of the lines in `_quarto.yml`
- [ ] The date the files were last edited

::: {.feedback}
File numbers only help you keep the *Files* panel tidy. The sidebar follows the
list in the settings file, so reordering means moving a line.
:::
:::

A chapter should take a learner roughly [?]{.fitb answer="20" tol="10"} minutes.
(Type a number of minutes and click elsewhere; anything from 10 to 30 counts.)
